title: Peripheral Nerves & the Autonomic Nervous System
summary: Roots, plexuses, nerves and the involuntary nervous system.

lessons.title: Spinal Nerves, Dermatomes & Myotomes

levels.kid:
Out of each side of your spinal cord comes a nerve, like branches off a tree trunk. You have 31 pairs!

Each nerve has a back root that brings in feelings and a front root that sends out move signals. They join together into one nerve.

Each nerve takes care of its own stripe of skin, called a dermatome. Picture your body painted in stripes, like a zebra. Each stripe belongs to one nerve.

Each nerve also moves its own group of muscles. So if a doctor finds which stripe is numb, they know which nerve is pinched.
levels.hs:
Each **spinal nerve** forms from two roots:

- **Dorsal (back) root**: carries **sensory** signals in; its nerve cell bodies sit in the **dorsal root ganglion**
- **Ventral (front) root**: carries **motor** signals out

The roots join in the **intervertebral foramen** (the gap between vertebrae) to form a mixed spinal nerve, which splits into a **dorsal ramus** (back muscles and skin) and a **ventral ramus** (front of the body and the limbs). The ventral rami of the neck and lower back join into networks called **plexuses**.

A **dermatome** is the strip of skin supplied by one spinal nerve. Useful landmarks:
- **C6**: thumb · **C7**: middle finger · **C8**: little finger
- **T4**: nipple line · **T10**: belly button
- **L4**: inner shin and knee · **L5**: top of the foot and big toe · **S1**: outer foot and sole
- **S2–S4**: the "saddle" area

A **myotome** is the group of muscles one root controls:
- **C5**: shoulder abduction · **C6**: wrist extension · **C7**: elbow extension · **C8**: finger flexion · **T1**: spreading fingers
- **L2**: hip flexion · **L3**: knee extension · **L4**: ankle dorsiflexion · **L5**: big toe extension · **S1**: plantarflexion (standing on tiptoes)

A slipped disc in the lower back usually pinches one root, causing pain shooting down the leg (**sciatica**) plus numbness in that root's dermatome. Shingles, a reactivated chickenpox virus, causes a painful rash in a single dermatome.
levels.college:
**Structure.** Dorsal rootlets (cell bodies in the **DRG**, pseudounipolar) and ventral rootlets (axons of ventral horn alpha and gamma motor neurons, plus preganglionic autonomic fibers at T1–L2 and S2–S4) join in or near the intervertebral foramen. The mixed nerve gives a **meningeal (recurrent) branch**, **dorsal ramus** (deep back muscles, facet joints, overlying skin) and **ventral ramus**. At T1–L2, **white rami communicantes** carry myelinated preganglionic fibers to the sympathetic chain; **gray rami** at every level return unmyelinated postganglionic fibers.

**Dermatomes.** Maps (Foerster, Keegan and Garrett) differ because adjacent dermatomes **overlap**, so a single root lesion often produces only partial sensory loss, best detected with pinprick. Key points: C2 occiput, C3–C4 neck and cape, C5 lateral arm, C6 thumb and lateral forearm, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger and medial forearm, T1 medial arm, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L1 inguinal ligament, L3 anterior thigh to knee, L4 medial leg and medial malleolus, L5 dorsum of foot and great toe, S1 lateral foot and heel, S2–S4 perianal.

**Myotomes and reflexes** pair up: C5 (deltoid, biceps reflex), C6 (wrist extensors, brachioradialis reflex), C7 (triceps, triceps reflex), C8 (finger flexors), T1 (interossei); L2 (iliopsoas), L3–L4 (quadriceps, knee jerk), L4 (tibialis anterior), L5 (extensor hallucis longus, hip abductors, tibialis posterior), S1 (gastrocnemius, ankle jerk).

**Disc herniation rules.** A posterolateral lumbar herniation compresses the **traversing** root: L4–L5 disc → **L5** root; L5–S1 disc → **S1** root. A far-lateral herniation hits the **exiting** root (L4–L5 → L4). In the cervical spine, the root exits above its vertebra: C5–C6 disc → **C6** root.
levels.phd:
**Segmental embryology.** Dermatomes and myotomes reflect the segmental origin of somites. Each somite gives a dermomyotome (dermis and skeletal muscle) and a sclerotome (vertebrae). Sclerotomes resegment: each vertebra forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome and the cranial half of the next, so the spinal nerve, which grows out opposite the original somite, ends up between vertebrae at the intervertebral foramen. Neural crest cells migrate through the rostral half of each sclerotome (repelled by ephrins and semaphorins in the caudal half), producing segmented DRGs. Limb buds rotate during development, which twists the limb dermatomes: the upper limb's preaxial border (C5–C6, thumb) and the lower limb's medial rotation produce the spiral dermatome pattern of the leg.

**Mapping controversy.** Classic charts drew discrete bands, but intraoperative root stimulation and compressive radiculopathy data show large interindividual variability and overlap; the Lee 2008 evidence-based map shows only areas of consistent autonomous innervation. Prefixed and postfixed brachial plexuses shift the whole map by a segment.

**Dorsal root ganglion biology.** The DRG lies outside the blood-brain barrier with fenestrated capillaries, making it vulnerable to toxins (platinum agents, pyridoxine excess) and autoimmune attack. Its location also explains a key electrodiagnostic rule: in a **preganglionic** lesion (root avulsion proximal to the DRG), the sensory axon remains connected to its cell body, so **sensory nerve action potentials are preserved** despite anesthesia; in a postganglionic lesion they disappear.

**Radicular pain mechanisms.** Pain from disc herniation arises not only from compression but from chemical radiculitis: nucleus pulposus exposure releases TNF-alpha and other cytokines that sensitize the DRG and root, explaining severe pain with small herniations and the efficacy of anti-inflammatory approaches.
levels.expert:
**The radiculopathy workup.** Combine pain distribution, dermatomal sensory loss, myotomal weakness and reflexes; any single finding is weak alone.

**Lumbar classics:**
- **L4**: medial leg numbness, weak quadriceps and dorsiflexion, reduced knee jerk
- **L5**: numb dorsum of foot and great toe, weak great toe extension, dorsiflexion, **hip abduction** and **ankle inversion**; reflexes usually normal
- **S1**: numb lateral foot and sole, weak plantarflexion (test with repeated single-leg toe raises), reduced ankle jerk

**Cervical classics:** C6 (thumb numbness, weak biceps and wrist extension, reduced brachioradialis reflex), C7 (most common; middle finger, weak triceps, reduced triceps reflex), C8 (little finger, weak grip).

**Distinguishing an L5 root from a peroneal neuropathy** at the fibular head: both cause foot drop, but weak **inversion** (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve) or **hip abduction** points to L5. EMG of paraspinal muscles helps: denervation there implicates the root.

**Management principles:**
- Most disc herniations improve without surgery over weeks; many shrink on follow-up imaging
- Red flags requiring urgent imaging: progressive weakness, cauda equina symptoms, fever or immunosuppression (epidural abscess), cancer history, major trauma
- **Microdiscectomy** speeds recovery of leg pain when it persists, and is indicated urgently for progressive deficit or cauda equina; long-term outcomes with or without surgery converge for many patients (SPORT trial)
- **Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion** or cervical disc arthroplasty treat refractory cervical radiculopathy

Pitfall: always check the level count on imaging. Transitional lumbosacral vertebrae (sacralized L5 or lumbarized S1) cause wrong-level surgery. Count from C2 down on a whole-spine sagittal image.

keyPoints: Dorsal root = sensory (cell bodies in the DRG); ventral root = motor; they join into a mixed spinal nerve
Ventral rami form plexuses; dorsal rami supply the back
Dermatome landmarks: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot
Myotomes: C5 shoulder abduction, C7 elbow extension, L3 knee extension, L4 dorsiflexion, L5 great toe extension, S1 plantarflexion
A posterolateral L4–L5 disc compresses the L5 root; L5–S1 compresses S1; C5–C6 compresses C6
Shingles follows a single dermatome

lessons.title: The Brachial Plexus

levels.kid:
The nerves for your arm start as five wires coming out of your neck.

Before they go down the arm, they mix and swap and braid together, like a messy plate of spaghetti. This braid is called the brachial plexus.

At the end, five main nerves come out. One bends your elbow. One lifts your arm out to the side. One straightens your wrist. Two control your hand and fingers.

Because the wires are mixed, losing one wire doesn't knock out a whole muscle. Clever!
levels.hs:
The **brachial plexus** is the network of nerves that supplies the arm. It forms from the ventral rami of **C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1**.

It has five parts, remembered as "**R**andy **T**ravis **D**rinks **C**old **B**eer": **Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords, Branches**.

- **Roots**: C5–T1
- **Trunks**: upper (C5–C6), middle (C7), lower (C8–T1)
- **Divisions**: each trunk splits into front and back divisions behind the collarbone
- **Cords**: lateral, posterior and medial, named by their position around the axillary artery
- **Branches**: the five main nerves

The **five terminal nerves**:
- **Musculocutaneous**: bends the elbow (biceps)
- **Axillary**: lifts the arm out to the side (deltoid)
- **Radial**: straightens the elbow, wrist and fingers; damage causes **wrist drop**
- **Median**: forearm flexors and thumb muscles; compressed in **carpal tunnel syndrome**
- **Ulnar**: most small hand muscles; damage causes a **claw hand**; it is the "funny bone" nerve

**Birth injuries:** if a baby's head and shoulder are pulled apart during a hard delivery, the upper trunk (C5–C6) can stretch, causing **Erb palsy**: the arm hangs by the side, turned inward, with the palm facing back (the "waiter's tip" position). Pulling the arm up hard can injure the lower trunk (C8–T1), causing **Klumpke palsy**, which affects the hand.
levels.college:
**Organization.** Roots C5–T1 lie between the anterior and middle scalenes; trunks in the posterior triangle of the neck; divisions behind the clavicle; cords in the axilla around the second part of the axillary artery; branches from the cords.

**Branches by level:**
- Roots: **dorsal scapular** (C5; rhomboids, levator scapulae), **long thoracic** (C5–C7; serratus anterior; winging), contribution to the phrenic nerve (C5)
- Upper trunk: **suprascapular** (C5–C6; supraspinatus, infraspinatus), nerve to subclavius
- Lateral cord: **musculocutaneous**, lateral pectoral, lateral root of median
- Medial cord: **ulnar**, medial pectoral, medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm, medial root of median
- Posterior cord: **axillary**, **radial**, upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal (latissimus dorsi)

**Terminal nerve functions:**
- **Musculocutaneous**: coracobrachialis, biceps, brachialis; lateral forearm skin
- **Axillary**: deltoid, teres minor; "regimental badge" skin over the deltoid
- **Radial**: triceps, brachioradialis, wrist and finger extensors, supinator
- **Median**: most forearm flexors, pronators, thenar muscles (LOAF: lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis)
- **Ulnar**: flexor carpi ulnaris, medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, hypothenar muscles, interossei, medial two lumbricals, adductor pollicis

**Lesion patterns:**
- **Upper trunk (Erb)**: loss of shoulder abduction, external rotation, elbow flexion and supination; arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated
- **Lower trunk (Klumpke)**: intrinsic hand weakness, claw hand, medial forearm numbness, possible **Horner syndrome** if T1 fibers to the sympathetic chain are injured; causes include traction with the arm abducted, cervical rib and **Pancoast tumor**
- **Thoracic outlet syndrome**: compression of the lower trunk or subclavian vessels
levels.phd:
**Variation and its consequences.** The plexus is **prefixed** (significant C4 contribution, often with a small T1) or **postfixed** (T2 contribution, smaller C5) in a notable minority, shifting expected myotomes and confounding level localization. Communications between median and musculocutaneous nerves in the arm, and between median and ulnar nerves in the forearm (**Martin–Gruber anastomosis**, present in a substantial minority), can make an ulnar lesion spare intrinsic hand muscles or produce confusing nerve conduction findings, such as an apparent conduction block in the forearm.

**Traumatic brachial plexus injury biomechanics.** High-energy traction (motorcycle crashes) increases the head-shoulder angle, injuring upper roots first; with the arm hyperabducted, lower roots fail. Roots are vulnerable at the foramen because ventral and dorsal rootlets lack epineurium and perineurium within the dura; upper roots have stronger ligamentous attachments to transverse processes, so lower roots (C8, T1) more often avulse from the cord, while upper roots more often rupture distally.

**Preganglionic versus postganglionic injury** determines repair options:
- Preganglionic signs: Horner syndrome (T1), winged scapula (long thoracic), weak rhomboids (dorsal scapular), elevated hemidiaphragm (phrenic), **preserved SNAPs** with anesthesia, pseudomeningocele on CT myelography or MRI
- Avulsed roots cannot be grafted from the spinal side, because there is no proximal stump

**Nerve transfer revolution.** Instead of long grafts, surgeons now transfer expendable fascicles near the target muscle: **Oberlin transfer** (an ulnar nerve fascicle to the biceps branch of the musculocutaneous nerve), double fascicular transfer (adding a median fascicle to the brachialis branch), spinal accessory to suprascapular, and triceps branch of radial to axillary. Short regeneration distances reach muscle before motor end plates degrade, improving outcomes compared with grafts from proximal stumps.
levels.expert:
**Examining a flail or weak arm after trauma.** Work proximal to distal and ask three questions: is the lesion pre- or postganglionic, which elements are involved, and is it improving?

- **Roots**: test rhomboids (dorsal scapular) and serratus anterior (long thoracic). If they are weak, the lesion is at the root level, close to the spinal cord
- **Horner syndrome** with a flail arm suggests T1 avulsion: poor prognosis for spontaneous recovery
- **Upper trunk**: weak supraspinatus and infraspinatus (suprascapular) plus deltoid and biceps
- **Cords**: posterior cord lesions spare rhomboids and serratus but hit deltoid, latissimus, triceps and wrist extensors

**Timing and investigations:**
- Open sharp lacerations: explore and repair early
- Closed traction injuries: obtain baseline imaging (MRI or CT myelography for pseudomeningoceles) and EMG at about 3–4 weeks, then reassess; if no clinical or electrical recovery by about 3–6 months, explore and reconstruct
- Reconstruction priorities: **elbow flexion** first, then shoulder abduction and external rotation, then hand function
- Free functional muscle transfer (for example gracilis) helps late presentations when native muscles have lost reinnervation potential

**Neonatal brachial plexus palsy:** most infants recover; absent biceps recovery by about 3–6 months (depending on the protocol) is a common trigger for surgical exploration and grafting or transfers.

**Iatrogenic risks:** interscalene nerve blocks can cause phrenic paresis; first rib resection and axillary surgery risk the lower trunk and cords; improper positioning during long operations can stretch the plexus.

Pitfall: in a trauma patient with a flail arm, check the subclavian artery and pulses. Vascular injury frequently accompanies severe plexus injury and must be fixed first.

keyPoints: The brachial plexus forms from C5–T1 ventral rami: roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches
Trunks: upper C5–C6, middle C7, lower C8–T1; cords named around the axillary artery
Terminal nerves: musculocutaneous (elbow flexion), axillary (deltoid), radial (extensors), median (forearm flexors, thenar), ulnar (intrinsic hand)
Erb palsy (upper trunk) = waiter's tip; Klumpke palsy (lower trunk) = claw hand ± Horner
Preganglionic avulsion signs: Horner, winged scapula, preserved SNAPs; nerve transfers have transformed repair

lessons.title: The Lumbosacral Plexus

levels.kid:
Your legs have their own nerve braid, down low in your back and hips.

The front part makes a nerve that straightens your knee, so you can kick a ball. Another nerve squeezes your legs together.

The back part makes the biggest nerve in your whole body: the sciatic nerve. It's about as thick as your thumb! It runs down the back of your leg and controls your foot and toes.

That's why nurses give shots in the upper outer part of the bottom: to stay far away from the big sciatic nerve.
levels.hs:
The legs get their nerves from the **lumbosacral plexus**, made of the **lumbar plexus** (about L1–L4) and the **sacral plexus** (about L4–S4).

**Lumbar plexus (front and inner thigh):**
- **Femoral nerve** (L2–L4): straightens the knee (quadriceps), helps flex the hip, carries the knee-jerk reflex; its branch the **saphenous nerve** gives feeling to the inner leg
- **Obturator nerve** (L2–L4): squeezes the thighs together (adductors)
- **Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve**: feeling on the outer thigh; squeezing it under a tight belt causes burning numbness called **meralgia paresthetica**

**Sacral plexus (back of the leg, buttock and foot):**
- **Sciatic nerve** (L4–S3): the largest nerve in the body; powers the hamstrings, then splits above the knee into the **tibial nerve** and the **common fibular (peroneal) nerve**
- **Tibial nerve**: points the foot down, curls the toes, feeling on the sole
- **Common fibular nerve**: lifts the foot and toes up; it wraps around the bony bump below the outer knee, where it is easily compressed, causing **foot drop**
- **Superior gluteal nerve**: hip abductors that keep the pelvis level while you walk
- **Inferior gluteal nerve**: gluteus maximus, for climbing stairs and standing up
- **Pudendal nerve** (S2–S4): pelvic floor and continence

Doctors test these by asking you to kick, walk on your heels and toes, and stand on one leg.
levels.college:
**Lumbar plexus** (ventral rami of L1–L4, often T12), formed within psoas major:
- **Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal** (L1): lower abdominal wall and groin skin
- **Genitofemoral** (L1–L2): cremaster (cremasteric reflex), skin of the genital region and upper thigh
- **Lateral femoral cutaneous** (L2–L3): anterolateral thigh; entrapment under the inguinal ligament = meralgia paresthetica (purely sensory)
- **Femoral** (L2–L4): iliacus, pectineus, sartorius, quadriceps; saphenous branch to the medial leg
- **Obturator** (L2–L4): adductor longus, brevis and magnus (part), gracilis; medial thigh skin

**Sacral plexus** (L4–S4; L4–L5 joins as the **lumbosacral trunk**):
- **Superior gluteal** (L4–S1): gluteus medius and minimus, tensor fasciae latae; lesion → **Trendelenburg sign** (pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg)
- **Inferior gluteal** (L5–S2): gluteus maximus; difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs
- **Sciatic** (L4–S3): exits through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis; hamstrings and part of adductor magnus
  - **Tibial**: gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior (inversion), long toe flexors, intrinsic foot muscles; sole of foot
  - **Common fibular**: deep branch (tibialis anterior, toe extensors; first web space skin) and superficial branch (fibularis longus and brevis, eversion; dorsum of foot)
- **Pudendal** (S2–S4): external anal and urethral sphincters, perineal skin
- Posterior femoral cutaneous (S1–S3): posterior thigh

**Lesion pearls:**
- **Common fibular palsy** at the fibular neck (leg crossing, casts, weight loss, prolonged squatting): weak dorsiflexion and eversion, inversion preserved, sensory loss on the dorsum
- **Femoral neuropathy** (retroperitoneal hematoma, pelvic surgery): weak knee extension, absent knee jerk, buckling knee
- Sciatic injury from hip arthroplasty or misplaced gluteal injection mainly affects the fibular division
levels.phd:
**Why the fibular division is so vulnerable.** Within the sciatic nerve, the common fibular fascicles have fewer, larger fascicles with less protective connective tissue, are tethered at the sciatic notch and fibular neck, and lie more laterally and superficially. During hip surgery, traction or compression therefore produces a deficit that can look exactly like an isolated fibular neuropathy, and electrodiagnosis (short head of biceps femoris, the only thigh muscle supplied by the fibular division) distinguishes a high sciatic lesion from a fibular neck lesion.

**Lumbosacral plexopathy.** Unlike radiculopathy, plexopathy produces deficits spanning multiple roots and nerves without paraspinal denervation, since dorsal rami branch off proximally. Causes include retroperitoneal hematoma (often with anticoagulation), malignancy (colorectal, cervical, lymphoma), radiation plexopathy (painless, with myokymic discharges on EMG, developing years later), and **diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy** (diabetic amyotrophy), a microvasculitis causing severe asymmetric thigh pain, weight loss and proximal weakness, typically in older people with relatively well-controlled type 2 diabetes. Pathology shows ischemic injury with perivascular inflammation, and recovery is slow over months.

**Piriformis syndrome debate.** Anatomical variation in which part or all of the sciatic nerve pierces the piriformis is common in cadavers, yet its causal role in buttock pain remains controversial because clinical criteria are inconsistent; MR neurography and diagnostic injections have refined but not settled it.

**Pudendal neurophysiology.** The pudendal nerve carries the afferent and efferent limbs of the bulbocavernosus and anal reflexes and voluntary sphincter control; injury during childbirth contributes to fecal incontinence, and its sacral origin explains why conus and cauda equina lesions abolish these reflexes.
levels.expert:
**The foot drop algorithm.** Foot drop is a symptom with a long differential; localize it before ordering imaging.

- **Common fibular neuropathy**: weak dorsiflexion and eversion, **normal inversion**, normal ankle jerk, sensory loss over the dorsum and first web space, Tinel at the fibular neck
- **L5 radiculopathy**: weak dorsiflexion and **inversion** and **hip abduction**, often back pain radiating down the leg, paraspinal denervation on EMG
- **Sciatic neuropathy**: adds weak hamstrings and plantarflexion; consider recent hip surgery, prolonged immobility, gluteal compartment syndrome, or a mass
- **Lumbosacral plexopathy**: multi-nerve involvement, often with pain and weight loss
- **Central causes**: a parasagittal frontal lesion (meningioma near the motor leg area), or motor neuron disease; look for UMN signs

**Management:**
- Compressive fibular palsy usually recovers with removal of pressure; provide an **ankle-foot orthosis** to prevent tripping
- If no recovery after about 3–4 months, consider exploration and decompression at the fibular neck; for complete persistent palsy, a **tibialis posterior tendon transfer** restores dorsiflexion
- Nerve laceration from knee dislocation needs vascular assessment and early surgical planning

**Femoral and obturator nerves in surgery:** lithotomy positioning and pelvic retractors can compress the femoral nerve; lateral lumbar interbody fusion through psoas risks the genitofemoral nerve and lumbar plexus, monitored with EMG during surgery.

**Injection safety:** gluteal intramuscular injections are placed in the upper outer quadrant or the ventrogluteal site to avoid the sciatic nerve; injection injury causes immediate severe pain and deficit, and should be explored if it does not improve.

Pitfall: painless foot drop with brisk reflexes is not a fibular palsy. Image the brain or spinal cord.

keyPoints: Lumbar plexus (L1–L4) gives femoral (knee extension, knee jerk) and obturator (adduction) nerves
Sacral plexus (L4–S4) gives the sciatic, gluteal and pudendal nerves
Sciatic splits into tibial (plantarflexion, inversion, sole) and common fibular (dorsiflexion, eversion, dorsum)
Common fibular palsy at the fibular neck causes foot drop with inversion spared; L5 radiculopathy weakens inversion
Superior gluteal nerve lesion causes a Trendelenburg sign
Meralgia paresthetica = lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment

lessons.title: Sympathetic & Parasympathetic Systems

levels.kid:
Your body has an autopilot. It runs things you don't think about, like your heartbeat, sweating and digesting food.

The autopilot has two modes.

Fight-or-flight mode is for scary moments. Your heart races, your eyes open wide, and you get ready to run.

Rest-and-digest mode is for calm moments. Your heart slows down, your tummy digests lunch, and your mouth makes spit.

The two modes are like a gas pedal and a brake, working together to keep you balanced.
levels.hs:
The **autonomic nervous system** controls involuntary functions: heart rate, blood pressure, breathing passages, digestion, sweating, pupils and the bladder. It has two main branches:

**Sympathetic ("fight or flight")**
- Comes out of the spinal cord at **T1–L2** (thoracolumbar)
- Speeds the heart, raises blood pressure, widens airways and pupils, shifts blood to muscles, slows digestion, and causes sweating
- The **adrenal medulla** releases **adrenaline (epinephrine)** into the blood

**Parasympathetic ("rest and digest")**
- Comes from **cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X** and the **sacral cord S2–S4** (craniosacral)
- Slows the heart, narrows pupils, increases saliva and digestion, and empties the bladder
- The **vagus nerve (CN X)** carries most parasympathetic signals to the chest and abdomen

Both use a **two-neuron chain**: one neuron from the brain or cord to a ganglion, then a second neuron to the organ. The chemical messengers differ: the first neurons in both systems use **acetylcholine**; the second sympathetic neuron mostly uses **norepinephrine**, while the second parasympathetic neuron uses **acetylcholine**.

The **hypothalamus** is the autonomic system's control center.

A classic clinical sign: **Horner syndrome**, from damage to the sympathetic pathway to the face, causes a droopy eyelid, a small pupil and reduced sweating on one side.
levels.college:
**Sympathetic anatomy.** Preganglionic neurons in the **intermediolateral cell column (T1–L2)** exit through ventral roots and **white rami communicantes** to the **paravertebral chain**, where they synapse, ascend or descend, or pass through as **splanchnic nerves** to **prevertebral ganglia** (celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric). Preganglionic fibers are short, postganglionic long. Cervical ganglia (superior, middle, cervicothoracic/stellate) supply the head and upper limbs.

**Parasympathetic anatomy.** Long preganglionic, short postganglionic, with ganglia near or in the target:
- **CN III** (Edinger–Westphal) → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae, ciliary muscle
- **CN VII** → pterygopalatine (lacrimal) and submandibular ganglia
- **CN IX** → otic ganglion → parotid
- **CN X** → intramural ganglia of thoracic and abdominal viscera to about the splenic flexure
- **S2–S4 pelvic splanchnic nerves** → hindgut, bladder detrusor, erectile tissue

**Neurotransmission.** All preganglionic neurons release **ACh** onto **nicotinic (Nn)** receptors. Parasympathetic postganglionic release ACh onto **muscarinic** receptors. Sympathetic postganglionic release **norepinephrine** onto adrenergic receptors (alpha-1 vasoconstriction, beta-1 cardiac, beta-2 bronchodilation), except **sweat glands** (cholinergic, muscarinic). The **adrenal medulla** is a modified ganglion releasing mainly epinephrine.

**Bladder:** sympathetic (T11–L2, hypogastric) relaxes detrusor and contracts the internal sphincter (storage); parasympathetic (S2–S4) contracts detrusor (voiding); pudendal (somatic) controls the external sphincter; the **pontine micturition center** coordinates.

**Horner syndrome:** ptosis (superior tarsal muscle), miosis, anhidrosis. Three-neuron pathway: hypothalamus → ciliospinal center (C8–T2) → superior cervical ganglion → along the internal carotid → dilator pupillae.
levels.phd:
**Beyond antagonism.** The textbook push-pull model holds for the heart and pupil, but many organs receive only one division (most blood vessels, sweat glands and piloerector muscles receive only sympathetic input), and in others the divisions cooperate (sexual function requires parasympathetic erection and sympathetic emission). Autonomic outflow is organ-specific and patterned, not a global switch: thermoregulatory, cardiovascular and gut pathways are controlled independently by distinct premotor neurons in the rostral ventrolateral medulla, raphe and paraventricular hypothalamus.

**Cotransmission.** Sympathetic terminals co-release ATP and neuropeptide Y with norepinephrine; parasympathetic fibers co-release VIP and nitric oxide, which mediate vasodilation and gut sphincter relaxation. These explain atropine-resistant components of vagal responses.

**Central autonomic network.** Insular and anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, parabrachial nucleus, nucleus of the solitary tract (the main visceral afferent hub) and ventrolateral medulla form a reciprocally connected network. The **baroreflex** runs from carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X) afferents to NTS, which excites nucleus ambiguus vagal neurons and, via caudal ventrolateral medulla, inhibits RVLM sympathetic premotor neurons.

**The enteric nervous system**, with hundreds of millions of neurons in myenteric and submucosal plexuses, can run peristalsis independently and communicates bidirectionally with the CNS via vagal afferents, a pathway now studied in the gut-brain axis, including the hypothesis that alpha-synuclein pathology in Parkinson disease may begin in the gut and spread via the vagus.

**Autonomic failure** distinguishes peripheral (pure autonomic failure, autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy with ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies) from central (multiple system atrophy) disease; cardiac sympathetic imaging is abnormal in Lewy body disorders but typically preserved in MSA.
levels.expert:
**Autonomic problems a neurosurgeon manages:**

- **Neurogenic shock** after cervical or high thoracic cord injury: hypotension with bradycardia from lost sympathetic outflow and intact vagal tone. Distinguish it from hemorrhagic shock (tachycardia). Treat with fluids, vasopressors with beta activity, and atropine or pacing for severe bradycardia; airway suctioning can trigger dangerous bradycardia
- **Autonomic dysreflexia** (injuries at or above T6): a stimulus below the lesion (full bladder, constipation, pressure sore) triggers unopposed sympathetic reflexes with severe hypertension; baroreceptor-driven vagal bradycardia and flushing above the level follow. Sit up, remove tight clothing, check the catheter and bowel, and treat persistent hypertension
- **Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity** after severe traumatic brain injury: episodes of tachycardia, hypertension, fever, sweating and posturing; a diagnosis of exclusion after infection and seizures

**Localizing Horner syndrome:**
- First-order (central): lateral medullary stroke, cord lesions above T2, syrinx
- Second-order (preganglionic): **Pancoast tumor**, neck surgery or trauma, lower brachial plexus avulsion
- Third-order (postganglionic): **internal carotid dissection** (painful Horner: an emergency because of stroke risk), cavernous sinus lesions, cluster headache. Facial sweating is largely spared because sudomotor fibers to most of the face travel with the external carotid
- Pharmacologic testing: apraclonidine reverses anisocoria in Horner (denervation supersensitivity); hydroxyamphetamine helps separate pre- from postganglionic lesions

**Surgical sympathectomy:** endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy treats severe palmar hyperhidrosis; compensatory sweating elsewhere is the main drawback. Stellate ganglion block is used for complex regional pain and some arrhythmias.

Pitfall: new Horner syndrome with neck pain is a carotid dissection until imaging proves otherwise.

keyPoints: Sympathetic = thoracolumbar (T1–L2), short preganglionic, long postganglionic; mostly norepinephrine
Parasympathetic = craniosacral (CN III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4), long preganglionic, short postganglionic; acetylcholine
All preganglionic neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors; sweat glands are the cholinergic sympathetic exception
The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine into the blood
Horner syndrome = ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis from a lesion anywhere in the 3-neuron sympathetic pathway
The hypothalamus is the main autonomic control center

lessons.title: Common Nerve Injuries

levels.kid:
Nerves are like long electric cords running through your body. Sometimes they get squished, stretched or cut.

If you sit on your leg too long and it goes "pins and needles," that's a nerve getting squished for a little while. It wakes back up fast!

If a nerve gets badly hurt, it can regrow, but very slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow. A nerve in the arm might take months to heal.

If a nerve is cut all the way, a surgeon can sew the ends together, like fixing a broken cord, so it has a path to grow back.
levels.hs:
Peripheral nerves can be **compressed**, **stretched** or **cut**. Doctors sort injuries by severity:

- **Neurapraxia**: the mildest. The insulation (myelin) is damaged but the nerve fiber is intact. It recovers in days to weeks. (Like your foot "falling asleep," but longer.)
- **Axonotmesis**: the nerve fiber (axon) is broken but its tube of connective tissue is intact. The fiber regrows down the tube at about **1 millimeter a day** (about an inch a month).
- **Neurotmesis**: the whole nerve is cut. It usually needs **surgery**.

**Common injuries:**
- **Carpal tunnel syndrome** (median nerve at the wrist): numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, worse at night; weak thumb muscles in severe cases
- **Cubital tunnel syndrome** (ulnar nerve at the elbow): numb ring and little fingers, weak hand grip
- **Radial nerve palsy** (upper arm fracture or sleeping with the arm over a chair): **wrist drop**
- **Axillary nerve injury** (shoulder dislocation): weak shoulder lifting, numb patch on the shoulder
- **Common fibular nerve palsy** (pressure below the outer knee): **foot drop**

**Tinel sign:** tapping over a nerve causes tingling in its area, which can show where it is compressed or how far it has regrown.

Doctors test nerves with **nerve conduction studies and EMG**, which measure how fast and strongly signals travel and whether muscles have lost their nerve supply. Surgery can release a trapped nerve, sew a cut one, or use a graft from another nerve.
levels.college:
**Classification.**
- **Seddon:** neurapraxia (focal demyelination, conduction block, no Wallerian degeneration), axonotmesis (axonal disruption with intact endoneurium; Wallerian degeneration distally; regrowth along original tubes), neurotmesis (complete disruption)
- **Sunderland grades:** I neurapraxia; II axon; III axon + endoneurium (misdirected regrowth, incomplete recovery); IV + perineurium (scar, neuroma-in-continuity, needs surgery); V complete transection

**Wallerian degeneration and regeneration.** Distal axon and myelin break down over days; Schwann cells dedifferentiate, clear debris with macrophages and form **bands of Büngner** guiding regrowth at about 1 mm per day. Target muscle must be reached before **motor end plates** and denervated muscle irreversibly degenerate (roughly 12–18 months).

**Entrapment neuropathies:**
- **Carpal tunnel** (median): nocturnal paresthesia in the radial three and a half digits, thenar wasting; **palm sensation spared** (palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel); Phalen and Tinel signs; associated with pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis
- **Cubital tunnel** (ulnar at the elbow): little and ring finger numbness including dorsal hand, weak interossei, **Froment sign** (thumb IP flexion compensating for weak adductor pollicis)
- **Guyon canal** (ulnar at the wrist): spares dorsal hand sensation
- **Radial at the spiral groove** (humeral shaft fracture, "Saturday night palsy"): wrist and finger drop, triceps usually spared; **posterior interosseous** lesions spare sensation and wrist extension partly (finger drop)
- **Axillary** (anterior shoulder dislocation, surgical neck fracture)
- **Common fibular at fibular neck**: foot drop

**Electrodiagnosis:** NCS show focal slowing or conduction block in demyelination and reduced amplitudes in axonal loss. **Fibrillation potentials** on EMG appear about 2–3 weeks after axonal injury (once Wallerian degeneration reaches the muscle), so early studies can falsely look reassuring.
levels.phd:
**Molecular biology of regeneration.** Injury converts Schwann cells into a repair phenotype driven by the transcription factor **c-Jun**, which downregulates myelin genes and upregulates neurotrophic factors (GDNF, BDNF, NGF), cytokines that recruit macrophages, and adhesion molecules. Neurons switch from a transmitting to a growth state, upregulating regeneration-associated genes (ATF3, GAP-43, SOX11), triggered partly by retrograde injury signals carried by importins and dynein. Prolonged denervation erodes the repair phenotype: Schwann cells lose c-Jun expression and die, which explains why delayed repair and long distances fail even with good surgery.

**Specificity.** Motor axons preferentially reinnervate motor pathways (preferential motor reinnervation), but misdirection is common; in mixed nerves, motor axons growing into sensory tubes are wasted. Synkinesis after facial nerve injury and co-contraction after brachial plexus repair are clinical outcomes of misdirected regeneration.

**Accelerating recovery.** Brief low-frequency **electrical stimulation** of the proximal stump at the time of repair upregulates BDNF and trkB and accelerates axon outgrowth across the repair site; randomized trials in carpal tunnel release and digital nerve repair show faster recovery. Other approaches include conditioning lesions, tacrolimus (neuroregenerative in animals), and processed nerve allografts and conduits for short gaps.

**Ultrasound and MR neurography** now image nerves directly: enlarged cross-sectional area at the carpal tunnel correlates with electrodiagnostic severity, and MR neurography shows T2 hyperintensity and denervation edema in muscles within days, earlier than EMG fibrillations.

**Mononeuritis multiplex**, sequential infarction of individual nerves from vasculitis, diabetes or infection, is a reminder that a patient with several unrelated nerve palsies needs a systemic workup, often including nerve biopsy.
levels.expert:
**Surgical decision-making for nerve injury.**

- **Sharp, clean laceration with a deficit**: explore and repair primarily within days; tension-free epineurial or group fascicular coaptation under magnification
- **Blunt or contused laceration**: tag the ends and repair at about 3 weeks, once the zone of injury declares itself, usually with a graft
- **Closed stretch or contusion injury** (most common): baseline exam, EMG at 3–4 weeks, repeat at about 3 months; if no clinical or electrical recovery, explore. **Intraoperative nerve action potentials** across a neuroma-in-continuity guide whether to neurolyse (NAP present) or resect and graft (NAP absent)
- **Gaps**: autografts (commonly the **sural nerve**) for longer gaps; conduits or allografts for short sensory gaps; **distal nerve transfers** when the distance to muscle is too long

**The clock:** muscle must be reinnervated within roughly a year to a year and a half. Estimate distance from injury to the target and divide by about 1 mm/day; if the math exceeds the window, consider a transfer early rather than waiting.

**Carpal tunnel release:** indicated for persistent symptoms despite splinting, thenar weakness or atrophy, or axonal loss on studies; open and endoscopic techniques have similar outcomes. Recurrent or failed cases warrant checking for incomplete release, a wrong diagnosis (C6 radiculopathy, double crush) or polyneuropathy.

**Iatrogenic injuries to avoid:** spinal accessory nerve in posterior triangle lymph node biopsy (trapezius weakness, shoulder droop), radial nerve in humeral plating, common fibular nerve with tight casts, ulnar nerve from elbow positioning during long surgery.

Pitfall: a normal EMG one week after injury does not mean the nerve is intact. Denervation changes take about 2–3 weeks to appear; repeat the study.

keyPoints: Seddon: neurapraxia (myelin, recovers quickly), axonotmesis (axon broken, tube intact), neurotmesis (nerve cut, needs surgery)
Axons regrow about 1 mm per day; muscle must be reinnervated within roughly 12–18 months
Carpal tunnel = median nerve at wrist; cubital tunnel = ulnar at elbow; spiral groove = radial (wrist drop); fibular neck = foot drop
Fibrillations on EMG appear 2–3 weeks after axonal injury
Tinel sign tracks compression sites and regrowth
Repair options: primary repair, sural nerve graft, nerve transfer
